REVIEW:
# Review: 2027 Customer Support Hiring Plan

## Overall

This is a strong memo. The decision comes first. The phasing argument (average vs. peak vs. off-peak) is clear and well reasoned. The arithmetic largely checks out against the brief. The most serious gaps are:

- The steady-state "54 covers 52" claim ignores attrition drag.
- The treatment of complaint backlogs during the peak creates compliance exposure.
- The vendor comparison is too generous.
- The plan contradicts the 8-person class cap.

None of these overturns the recommendation, but a careful COO will find several of them.

## Arithmetic check

These figures reproduce correctly from the brief:

| Claim | Check | Result |
|---|---|---|
| 36,800 avg tickets/month | 31,000 × 1.35 × 0.88 = 36,828 | ✓ |
| ~50 agents | 36,828 / 740 = 49.8 | ✓ |
| Complaint load ~2.4 agents | 9% × 36,800 = 3,312 × 6 min = 331 h / 140 = 2.37 | ✓ |
| Peak 51,600 / ~70 agents | 36,828 × 1.4 = 51,559 / 740 = 69.7 | ✓ |
| Off-peak ~13% below average | (12 × 36,828 − 3 × 51,559) / 9 = 31,893 → −13.4% | ✓ |
| Jan class productive Mar 22 | Jan 11 + 10 weeks | ✓ |
| $610k vs $816k | 8 × $68k × ~0.97 + 4 × $68k × ~0.3 ≈ $608k | ✓ |
| 16,000–17,500 peak shortfall | Feb: 51,559 − 46 × 740 = 17,520; Apr: ~17,000 after complaint load | ✓ (ignores attrition) |
| $7.66 in-house per ticket | $68k / 12 / 740 | ✓ |
| 2026 peak 28% short | 31,080 / 43,400 = 0.716 | ✓ |
| 6,600 Spanish tickets → 9 agents | 18% × 36,828 = 6,629 / 740 = 8.96 | ✓ |
| 18 leavers; 5 avoided at 28% | 38% / 28% of ~48 avg headcount | ✓ |

The numbers hold. The problems are in the assumptions and in what the model leaves out.

## Substantive issues

### 1. "54 covers 52" ignores attrition drag
This is the most important gap. Each of about 18 replacements loses about 5 productive weeks, which is about 90 agent-weeks, or **about 1.7 FTE a year**. That is before counting the vacancy gap between a departure and the next monthly class. Effective capacity is therefore about 51–52 against a need of about 52, with essentially no margin.

Early-tenure attrition is also usually well above 38%. Some of the January class will likely leave before the peak ends. The plan should model effective rather than nominal headcount.

### 2. The help-centre factor is probably double-counted and thinly evidenced
The help centre launched in September 2026, so the 2026 average of 31,000 already includes about 4 months of the effect. Applying the full 12% to that average overstates the reduction. Relative to the 2026 average, the factor is closer to 0.88 / 0.96 ≈ 0.92. That gives about **38,400 tickets/month**, roughly 2 more agents.

Separately, two months of data may reflect novelty. This belongs in the "Assumptions to confirm" section with a sensitivity range.

### 3. Growth timing is applied inconsistently
The memo says off-peak need rises from about 45 to 52 as users grow. But it sizes the Feb–Apr peak off the full-year average, even though tax season sits early on the growth curve. The peak is probably overstated and Q4 understated. Correcting this would shrink the vendor need and strengthen the case for the September class.

### 4. The 15-day complaint rule is a compliance risk, not only a handling-time cost
The plan absorbs unmet peak demand "as longer waits, as we did in 2026." Complaints cannot be outsourced, and from April 1 they cannot wait past 15 days. Peak complaint volume is about 4,600 a month, which needs about 3.3 agents for the added handling time alone, and it lands in April, the first month of the rule.

The plan needs an explicit rule that complaints are triaged first, with some capacity ring-fenced for them. It should also check whether misclassified complaints sent to the vendor would breach the rule.

### 5. The vendor case is too favourable and sits outside the headcount budget
The $4.10 vs $7.66 comparison omits several costs and risks:
- repeat contacts and escalations back in-house
- quality assurance and vendor management overhead
- data-security and compliance review, which matters for a payments app
- vendor onboarding lead time, since peak starts in about 11 weeks
- contract minimums
- whether the vendor can handle Spanish, where the gap is worst

The memo also implicitly sets the $206k underspend against the $150k vendor ask. The COO's budget covers *headcount*, so that money may not be fungible. Say so directly, or don't imply it.

### 6. The January class breaks the 8-person cap
The table schedules 8 net new hires plus 1–3 backfills in the January class, which is 9–11 people against a maximum of 8. Either some net hires move to February (where they would be only 50% productive during the peak), or January backfills are deferred.

The plan should also check trainer, QA, and team-lead capacity for back-to-back full classes during peak months.

### 7. No service-level target
The plan sizes headcount for throughput at 100% utilisation. With no wait-time target, queues will be long even when "capacity equals demand." This also weakens the claim that hiring all 12 in Q1 would leave the team "6–8 overstaffed." Some of that slack would show up as shorter waits, especially for Spanish tickets. State a target, even a rough one.

### 8. Spanish coverage is optimistic
- The plan reaches 10 bilingual agents against a need of 9, which leaves no margin for attrition. At 38%, it loses about 1–2 bilingual agents by Q2.
- Peak Spanish need is about 12–13 agents.
- Sourcing 6 or more bilingual hires with offers out by mid-December leaves about 4 weeks. That likely requires a language premium, which interacts with the existing pay complaints in exit interviews.
- The vendor's Spanish capability is unconfirmed.

### 9. The September gate has no decision criteria
The memo should define what Q2 result cancels, shrinks, or expands the September class, for example tickets per active user falling a further X%. Timing is also tight. Q2 features may have only a few weeks of data by the July review, and September offers need to go out around mid-August.

### 10. Shift allocation is not addressed
Exit interviews name night shifts as a driver of attrition, yet the plan doesn't say which shifts new hires will fill. If new hires are put on nights, early-tenure attrition will be worse.

### 11. Alternatives are only lightly compared
- All 12 in Q1 is dismissed but not costed. It would cost about $790k, close to the full $816k.
- Overtime or temporary staff are not considered as alternatives to the vendor.
- The cost of long waits, such as customer churn, is not estimated.
- The 2028 tax season, at likely 80 or more agents, deserves one forward-looking line.

## Minor / editorial

- **Length:** about 700 words against a 450–600 brief. The "Why this phasing" and "Attrition" sections could be tightened.
- **Voice:** the memo is from "Support Operations" but uses "I will bring a proposal." Choose one.
- **Stray formatting:** the document ends with an empty `---` / `##` heading. Remove it.
- **140 productive hours:** the complaint estimate depends on this figure. Cite its source, or show the result at 120 and 160 hours.
- **"Explains why Spanish waits are 3.4× longer":** this is plausible but asserted. In 2026, Spanish need was about 7.5 agents against 4 in place, a worthwhile number to show as support.

## Coverage against your anticipated points

This review covers all 13 points you expected. It also raises a few you didn't list:

- the steady-state attrition drag of about 1.7 FTE (issue 1)
- the partial double-counting of the help-centre effect (issue 2)
- the peak Spanish need and bilingual attrition (issue 8)
- the tight timing of the July review against September offers (issue 9)
- the editorial issues (length, voice, stray heading)
